course.title: Web Application Security
course.description: A defensive tour of how web applications are attacked and, more importantly, how to prevent it — injection, broken access control, weak authentication, and unsafe data handling. Structure draws on the ACM Computing Curricula security knowledge area and references the OWASP Top 10:2025 risk categories. Prevention and mitigation only.

questions.prompt: The single most reliable place to enforce a security rule in a web app is…
options: on the server, for every request
questions.explanation: The client is fully controllable by the user; only server-side checks are trustworthy.

questions.prompt: SQL injection is best prevented by…
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries keep data separate from code so input can never become SQL.

questions.prompt: Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when an app…
options: renders untrusted input as active HTML/JS
questions.explanation: XSS is an output-encoding failure: untrusted data is interpreted as markup or script.

questions.prompt: The #1 risk in the OWASP Top 10:2025 is…
questions.explanation: Broken Access Control remains ranked #1 in the 2025 list.

questions.prompt: Passwords should be stored…
options: encrypted so they can be decrypted
as a salted, slow one-way hash
questions.explanation: Use a slow salted hash (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2); passwords should never be recoverable.

questions.prompt: An 'insecure direct object reference' means a user can…
options: read another user's record by changing an ID
questions.explanation: It is a broken access control flaw: the server serves an object without checking ownership.

questions.prompt: TLS (HTTPS) primarily protects data…
options: in transit between client and server
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts and authenticates data while it moves across the network.

questions.prompt: Threat modeling is the practice of…
options: systematically identifying what could go wrong before building
questions.explanation: Threat modeling asks what you're building, what can go wrong, and what you'll do about it — early.

lessons.title: How web apps get attacked: the OWASP Top 10:2025
lessons.grammar_note: Golden rule: never trust input from the client — validate and authorize on the server.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the shape of the OWASP Top 10:2025 and why almost every web vulnerability comes back to *trust*. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, where is the only trustworthy place to enforce a rule?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A web app takes untrusted input (URLs, form fields, headers, cookies, files) and turns it into actions: database queries, HTML pages, files, redirects. An attack is simply input crafted so the app does something the developer didn't intend. The OWASP Top 10:2025 is the community's consensus list of the most critical categories: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection, A06 Insecure Design, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures, and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. Notice the pattern: the fix is almost never a single product — it is treating input as hostile and deciding, on the server, what is allowed. Example of the mindset: instead of asking 'is this input bad?' (a blocklist you will lose), ask 'is this input on my known-good allowlist?' — default deny, then permit the specific safe cases.

sections.heading: Worked example: reading the list defensively
Your turn
sections.text: For each scenario, name the OWASP:2025 category and one prevention: (1) a page echoes a URL parameter straight into HTML; (2) users can open /orders/1002 that isn't theirs; (3) the app ships with a default admin password; (4) errors that should block a payment instead let it through. Answers: (1) A05 Injection / XSS — output-encode and add a Content-Security-Policy; (2) A01 Broken Access Control — check ownership server-side, deny by default; (3) A02 Security Misconfiguration — remove defaults, force a strong credential on setup; (4) A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions — fail closed so errors block, never bypass, the check.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating security as a firewall you buy rather than decisions in your code. Mistake: relying on blocklists ('reject these bad words') instead of allowlists ('accept only this known-good set'). Exit: (a) What is the one word every web attack abuses? (b) Should access default to allow or deny? Answers: trust; deny.

lessons.title: Injection: preventing SQL injection and XSS
lessons.grammar_note: Never build SQL or HTML by concatenating user input — keep data and code separate.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize why injection happens and prevent the two most common forms — SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS). Warm-up: what makes untrusted input turn into runnable code?

sections.heading: The idea, with a vulnerable pattern and its fix
Worked examples of hardening code
Your turn
sections.text: Fix or classify each: (1) `db.query('DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = ' + id)`; (2) a comment field shown with `commentEl.innerHTML = text`; (3) reflecting `?msg=` directly into the page; (4) building a login query as `"... WHERE user='"+u+"' AND pass='"+p+"'"`. Answers: (1) parameterize: `db.query('DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = $1', [id])`; (2) use `textContent`, or sanitize/encode for HTML context; (3) output-encode `msg` and add a CSP — reflected XSS otherwise; (4) parameterize both fields AND verify the password against a stored hash, never compare in SQL.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: 'escaping' input by hand — you will miss a context (SQL vs HTML attribute vs JS vs URL each differ). Mistake: sanitizing input on the way in but forgetting to encode on the way out; encoding is context-specific and belongs at output. Mistake: trusting a hidden field or a dropdown because the UI 'limits' it — the client can send anything. Exit: (a) What separates data from code in a query? (b) Which DOM property renders text safely, `innerHTML` or `textContent`? Answers: a parameterized/prepared statement; textContent.

lessons.title: Access control and authorization flaws
lessons.grammar_note: Authenticate = who you are; authorize = what you may do. Check authorization on every request.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish authentication from authorization and prevent the #1 OWASP:2025 risk, Broken Access Control. Warm-up: if a user changes an ID in a URL, what must the server do before answering?

sections.heading: The idea, with a vulnerable pattern and its fix
Worked examples of hardening code
Your turn
sections.text: For each, state the flaw and the fix: (1) the 'Delete user' button is hidden for non-admins but the DELETE route has no role check; (2) `/account?id=57` shows whoever's account matches the id; (3) a JWT says `role: 'user'` and the server trusts a separate `?admin=true` query param; (4) rules are enforced only in React. Answers: (1) add a server-side role check — hiding UI is not authorization; (2) verify the id belongs to the session user, else 404; (3) never read privileges from client-supplied params — derive role from the verified session/token; (4) re-check every rule on the server; the client is advisory only.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing authentication with authorization — being logged in is not permission. Mistake: 'security through the UI' — hiding a button while the endpoint stays open. Mistake: fail-open defaults, where a missing check means 'allow'. Exit: (a) Which comes second, authentication or authorization? (b) When a check errors or is missing, should the system fail open or fail closed? Answers: authorization; fail closed (deny).

questions.prompt: The reliable, general fix for SQL injection is…
questions.explanation: Parameters keep user data out of the query's syntax.

questions.prompt: Assigning untrusted text to `innerHTML` risks…
questions.explanation: innerHTML can execute injected markup/script; use textContent or context-aware encoding.

questions.prompt: A user reads another account by changing an id in the URL. This is…
questions.explanation: The server served an object without checking ownership.

questions.prompt: Authorization should be enforced…
options: on the server for every request
once at login and never again
questions.explanation: Every request must be re-authorized server-side; the client can lie.

questions.prompt: A Content-Security-Policy header mainly helps by…
options: limiting what scripts/resources a page may load
questions.explanation: CSP is defense-in-depth that constrains injected scripts from running.

questions.prompt: 'Fail closed' means that when a check errors or is missing, the system…
questions.explanation: Safe default is to deny when in doubt.

lessons.title: Authentication and session security
lessons.grammar_note: Store password hashes (salted, slow), never the passwords themselves.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Protect logins and sessions: safe password storage, sensible multi-factor and lockout policy, and hardened cookies. Warm-up: why should a stored password never be decryptable?

sections.heading: The idea, with a vulnerable pattern and its fix
Worked examples of hardening code
Your turn
sections.text: Fix each weakness: (1) passwords stored with `sha1()`; (2) login says 'no such user' vs 'wrong password'; (3) the session cookie lacks HttpOnly and Secure; (4) the session id stays the same before and after login. Answers: (1) rehash with Argon2/bcrypt on next login and migrate; (2) return one generic message so accounts can't be enumerated; (3) set HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite; (4) regenerate the session id at login to prevent session fixation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: encrypting passwords 'so support can read them' — support should never be able to. Mistake: rolling your own token/crypto instead of a vetted library and session framework. Mistake: long-lived, non-rotating sessions with readable cookies. Exit: (a) Name one acceptable password-hashing algorithm. (b) Which cookie flag stops JavaScript from reading a session cookie? Answers: Argon2 (or bcrypt/scrypt); HttpOnly.

lessons.title: Secure data handling: encryption, secrets, and HTTPS
lessons.grammar_note: Protect data in transit (TLS) and at rest; keep secrets out of source code.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Protect sensitive data across its life: enforce HTTPS, encrypt at rest, and manage secrets so they never end up in your repo. Warm-up: what does TLS protect that database encryption does not?

sections.heading: The idea, with a vulnerable pattern and its fix
sections.text:
Cryptographic Failures (OWASP A04:2025) usually aren't broken math — they're data left unprotected or secrets left exposed. Two channels matter: *in transit* (network) and *at rest* (storage). And the fastest real-world leak is a secret hard-coded in the codebase.

Vulnerable (secret committed into source; plaintext transport):
```js
const DB_PASSWORD = 'S3cr3t!';       // hard-coded — leaks with the repo
fetch('http://api.internal/charge'); // plaintext HTTP over the network
```
Secure (load secrets from the environment/secret manager; require HTTPS):
```js
const DB_PASSWORD = process.env.DB_PASSWORD;   // injected at runtime, not stored
fetch('https://api.internal/charge');          // TLS in transit
// And redirect/upgrade all traffic to HTTPS + send HSTS:
res.set('Strict-Transport-Security', 'max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains');
```

sections.heading: Worked examples of hardening code
Your turn
sections.text: State the fix: (1) an API key pasted directly into a `.js` file; (2) a login form that posts over `http://`; (3) storing full credit-card numbers to 'save time later'; (4) using AES in ECB mode for structured data. Answers: (1) move it to an environment variable / secret manager and rotate the exposed key; (2) force HTTPS and add HSTS; (3) don't store it — tokenize via the payment processor and keep only what you need; (4) use an authenticated mode like AES-GCM with a unique IV per record, never ECB.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming HTTPS alone protects data at rest — it protects transit only. Mistake: committing `.env` files or keys 'temporarily'. Mistake: inventing your own cipher or reusing an IV. Exit: (a) Which protects data crossing the network, TLS or at-rest encryption? (b) Where should a database password live instead of the source code? Answers: TLS; an environment variable or secret manager.

items.translation: a database call that sends user data separately from the SQL text, so input can never become code
items.example: Using `WHERE email = $1` with a bound value prevents SQL injection.

items.translation: converting data to a safe representation for the context (HTML, attribute, JS, URL) at the moment it is rendered
items.example: Encoding `<` as `<` on output stops a comment from injecting a script tag.

items.translation: a flaw where the server fails to check whether a user is allowed to perform an action or reach an object
items.example: Reading /invoices/1002 that isn't yours is broken access control (an IDOR).

items.translation: a one-way password transform that adds a unique random salt, using a slow algorithm to resist cracking
items.example: Argon2 produces a salted hash so a leaked database doesn't reveal passwords.

items.translation: Transport Layer Security — the protocol behind HTTPS that encrypts and authenticates data in transit
items.example: TLS stops an attacker on the network from reading a login posted to the server.

items.translation: a structured review, done early, of what you're building, what could go wrong, and how you'll mitigate it
items.example: A threat model of a login flow flags credential stuffing before code is written.

questions.prompt: Passwords should be protected with…
questions.explanation: Slow, salted, one-way hashing resists cracking and can't be reversed.

questions.prompt: The HttpOnly cookie flag helps by…
questions.explanation: HttpOnly blocks script access, limiting session theft via XSS.

questions.prompt: TLS/HTTPS protects data primarily…
questions.explanation: TLS secures data as it moves between client and server.

questions.prompt: A database password belongs…
options: in an environment variable or secret manager
questions.explanation: Keep secrets out of source; inject them at runtime.

questions.prompt: Regenerating the session id at login prevents…
questions.explanation: A fresh id stops an attacker-set session from being reused after login.

questions.prompt: For data you must be able to recover, you should use…
options: AES-256-GCM with a unique IV per record
no encryption if you have HTTPS
questions.explanation: Authenticated encryption (GCM) with a unique IV protects data at rest.

lessons.title: Applied project: threat-model and harden a web app

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: You are handed the design of a small web app: a note-taking service where users sign up with email and password, create private notes, and share a note by link. There is an admin dashboard. Your job is to threat-model it and write a defensive hardening plan. You will NOT attack anything — you are the developer securing it before launch.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Data flow: list where untrusted input enters (signup, login, note body, share-link id, admin actions). 2) For at least four OWASP:2025 categories, name a concrete risk in THIS app and the specific prevention (e.g. Injection → parameterized queries + output encoding on note bodies; Broken Access Control → verify note ownership and admin role server-side; Authentication Failures → Argon2 hashing, MFA, session regeneration; Cryptographic Failures → HTTPS + HSTS, secrets from env, encrypt sensitive fields at rest). 3) Cookies & sessions: state your cookie flags and session lifetime. 4) Failure behavior: pick one error case and show it fails closed. 5) Secrets: describe how keys are stored and rotated.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Every input source is listed and treated as untrusted. ✔ Each risk names a specific, code-level prevention (not just 'be secure'). ✔ Access control is enforced server-side, deny-by-default, with ownership checks on the share link. ✔ Passwords are salted-hashed and cookies are HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite. ✔ Data is protected in transit and at rest, with no secrets in source. ✔ Your plan is entirely defensive — prevention and mitigation, no exploitation steps. If all six hold, you've thought like a security-minded engineer.
